query: Consider the following context: High entropy alloys have excellent wear resistance, so they have great application prospects in the fields of wear resistance and surface protection. In that context, which material can be used for adhere to the surface of a Cu matrix, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Depositing a thin layer of Cr on the surface of a Cu matrix will improve the adhesion of a High Entropy Alloy (HEA) coating, which is chosen for its excellent wear resistance and surface protection properties, to the Cu substrate.
generation.material_initial_state: Polycrystalline Cu matrix with a clean surface
generation.intervention: Deposit a 1-2 μm thick layer of Cr on the Cu surface using magnetron sputtering at 300°C
generation.conditions: Vacuum environment, 10^-5 mbar pressure, and 100 W power
generation.structural_mediator: Cr layer with a thickness of 1-2 μm
generation.mechanism: The Cr layer improves wettability by reducing the contact angle between the HEA coating and the Cu substrate, and enhances adhesion by forming a strong intermetallic bond between the Cr and Cu.
generation.predicted_outcome: Based on previous research on the effects of Cr layers on adhesion strength, we predict a 30% increase in adhesion strength, from 20 MPa to 26 MPa, as measured by scratch testing
generation.baseline: Adhesion strength of HEA coating on bare Cu substrate
generation.boundary: Based on industry standards and requirements for surface protection applications, an adhesion strength of 22 MPa is considered the minimum acceptable value, indicating sufficient improvement
generation.uncertainty: The actual adhesion strength may vary depending on the specific HEA coating composition, Cr layer thickness, and deposition conditions

falsification_experiment.design: Scratch testing of HEA coatings on Cu substrates with and without the Cr layer
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the adhesion strength of the HEA coating on the Cr-coated Cu substrate is less than 22 MPa, or if the scratch track morphology shows significant cracking or delamination (> 20% of the scratch track length), the hypothesis is falsified
